title: Monte Carlo pricing
objectives: Price an option by simulation and report its standard error.
Reduce the error with antithetic variates and price a path-dependent payoff.

screens.title: Eight futures
screens.prose: No tree this time. Draw possible prices for our share in a year, under the risk-neutral model. Here are eight draws, made by a C++ program with a fixed seed, with the call's payoff on each ($K = 100$, $r = 5\%$, $T = 1$).
screens.question: Estimate the call's price today from these eight paths, in pounds.

hints.text: Average the payoff column.
The payoffs add to £63.53 over eight paths.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Average all eight payoffs, then discount one year.

byKey.nodisc: That is the average payoff, paid in a year. Discount it: $7.94 \times e^{-0.05} = 7.55$.
byKey.bs: That is the Black-Scholes price. Eight paths give a much rougher answer; compute what they say.
byKey.itm: You averaged only the paths that paid. The other four paid £0 and count too.

explain.text: The payoffs average £7.94, worth $7.94e^{-0.05} = 7.55$ today. Eight paths are a poor sample: the true price is £10.45. More paths, and a measure of the error, are this lesson.

screens.title: Piling up paths
screens.prose: This chart repeats the experiment with 5,000 paths, in the browser's own random stream. The line is the running estimate: the discounted average payoff of the first $i$ paths. Slide to reveal it.
screens.question: As the paths pile up, how does the estimate behave?

options.text: It wobbles less and less, but still wobbles after thousands of paths
It lands exactly on £10.45 after a few hundred paths
options.why: Each new path moves the average a little, for ever. It gets close, never exactly there.
The early swings go both ways. There is no trend, only noise that shrinks.

options.text: It wobbles as much at the end as at the start
options.why: Late paths move an average of thousands only slightly. The swings shrink as the count grows.

hints.text: Compare the swings in the first 250 paths with those in the last 1,000.
One new path changes an average of $i$ paths by about $1/i$ of its payoff.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Reveal the whole line and compare its start with its end.

explain.text: One more path moves an average of $i$ paths by a fraction $1/i$ of its payoff, so the swings shrink. They shrink slowly, though: we will measure how slowly. A price from simulation needs its error beside it.

screens.title: Terminal prices
screens.prose: Under the risk-neutral model $$S_T = S\exp\!\big((r - \tfrac12\sigma^2)T + \sigma\sqrt T\,Z\big),$$ with $Z$ standard normal. As in level 1, seed one `std::mt19937` once and draw from one `std::normal_distribution<double>`, one draw per path, in order.
screens.question: Write `terminal_prices`.

tests.setup: std::vector<double> xs = terminal_prices(100.0, 0.05, 0.2, 1.0, 20000, 42u); double m = 0; for (double x : xs) m += x;

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB), and the first compile takes 10 to 15 s; later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs 6 hidden tests. Prices are compared within a relative 1e-9 with the values this compiler's libc++ gives for the same seed. `std::normal_distribution` is implementation-defined, so another library would give other draws.

hints.text: Make the generator and the distribution before the loop, once.
Work out the drift $(r - \sigma^2/2)T$ and $\sigma\sqrt T$ once too.
`out[i] = s * std::exp(drift + vol * z(gen));` with `std::mt19937 gen(seed);` and `std::normal_distribution<double> z(0.0, 1.0);`

feedback.correct: Reproducible draws: the same seed gives the same paths.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test under the editor.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 expects the first three draws of seed 42. Seed once, outside the loop, and draw exactly one `z(gen)` per path.
byKey.test-6: Test 6 averages 20,000 prices and expects about $100e^{0.05} = 105.13$. Check the drift: $(r - \sigma^2/2)T$, not $rT$.

explain.text: The $-\tfrac12\sigma^2$ makes the average $S_T$ grow at exactly $r$: here £105.17 against $100e^{0.05} = 105.13$. The seed fixes the whole stream, so a test can expect exact numbers. Those numbers are libc++'s; `std::normal_distribution` differs between libraries.

screens.title: The Monte Carlo price
screens.prose: The price is the discounted average payoff over many paths. Take the payoff as `const Payoff&`, as in lesson 5, so one function prices calls, puts and digitals. `terminal_prices` is loaded.
screens.question: Write `mc_price`.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB), and the first compile takes 10 to 15 s; later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs 6 hidden tests. Four prices are rounded to 4 places and compared with this compiler's values for the same seed. One test only asks that the 20,000-path call is within 3 standard errors (3 × 0.1042) of 10.4506.

hints.text: Get the terminal prices, add up `p(x)` over them, then average.
Discount once, at the end: `std::exp(-r * t)`.
`return std::exp(-r * t) * sum / n;`

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test under the editor.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 expects 10.4735. If you got 11.0105, you forgot to discount. If your digits differ, call `terminal_prices` with the same seed.
byKey.test-5: Test 5 has σ = 0: every path ends at £105.13, so the price is exactly $e^{-0.05} \times 5.13 = 4.8771$.

explain.text: 20,000 paths give £10.4735, £0.023 above Black-Scholes. With σ = 0 every path is the same, so the estimate is the discounted forward payoff exactly. The `Payoff&` argument means a new payoff class needs no new pricer.

screens.title: The standard error
screens.prose: A price without its error is half an answer. The **standard error** is $s/\sqrt n$, where $s$ is the sample standard deviation of the discounted payoffs, dividing by $n - 1$. With one path there is no spread to measure: throw.
screens.question: Write `mc_standard_error`.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB), and the first compile takes 10 to 15 s; later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs 5 hidden tests. Three errors are rounded to 4 places. One path must throw `std::invalid_argument`, which ends the program here.

hints.text: Two passes: first the mean of the discounted payoffs, then the squared deviations.
Divide the sum of squares by $n - 1$, then by $n$, then take the square root.
`return std::sqrt(ss / (n - 1) / n);` after `if (n < 2) throw std::invalid_argument("...");`

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test under the editor.

byKey.test-3: Test 3 uses two paths, paying £13.54 and £0. Dividing by $n - 1 = 1$ gives 6.7703; dividing by $n$ gives 4.7873.
byKey.test-5: Test 5 has one path. There is no spread to estimate: throw `std::invalid_argument` when `n < 2`.

explain.text: With 20,000 paths, $n$ against $n - 1$ changes nothing you can see; with two paths it is the difference between 6.77 and 4.79. Two passes avoid the cancellation of level 1: summing $y^2$ and subtracting $n\bar y^2$ gives 2.5e-8 instead of 0 when σ = 0.

screens.title: How fast the error falls
screens.prose: Your `mc_standard_error` for our call at six path counts, each four times the last. Same seed, so each run extends the one before.
screens.question: Our 20,000-path price has standard error £0.104. How many paths would give £0.052?

widget.label: Paths
widget.accept: 80,000: half the error needs four times the paths

hints.text: Compare neighbouring bars: what does four times the paths do?
Each bar is about half the one before.
Halving the error needs $2^2 = 4$ times the paths: $4 \times 20{,}000$.

feedback.correct: Four times the work for half the error.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read how much each ×4 in paths cuts the error.

byKey.double: Doubling the paths cuts the error only by $\sqrt 2$, to about £0.074. Halving needs four times.
byKey.root: You took $\sqrt 2$ times the paths. The error is $s/\sqrt n$, so it halves when $n$ is multiplied by 4.

explain.text: The error is $s/\sqrt n$: each four-fold increase halves it, bar after bar. So one more correct decimal place costs 100 times the paths. That slow rate is why variance reduction matters.

screens.title: Antithetic variates
screens.prose: $Z$ and $-Z$ are equally likely. For each draw, price the path with $Z$ and its mirror with $-Z$, and average the pair. When one is high the other tends to be low, so pair averages vary less. Write it with n draws, so 2n paths.
screens.question: Write `mc_price_antithetic`.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB), and the first compile takes 10 to 15 s; later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs 5 hidden tests. Prices are rounded to 4 places and compared with this compiler's values for seed 42. Draw one `z(gen)` per pair, in order.

hints.text: Draw `e = z(gen)` once per pair and use it twice.
The mirror path is `s * std::exp(drift - vol * e)`.
`sum += 0.5 * (p(s * std::exp(drift + vol * e)) + p(s * std::exp(drift - vol * e)));` then discount `sum / n`.

feedback.correct: Same work as 20,000 plain paths, smaller error.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test under the editor.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 expects 10.5031. Draw once per pair, not twice: the mirror reuses the same `e`.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 uses one pair. Its payoffs are £14.23 and £0 in a year: average them, then discount.

explain.text: For the same 20,000 payoffs, the standard error falls from £0.1042 to £0.0737: the variance halves, from 0.0109 to 0.0054. The pairs are negatively correlated because a call rises with $Z$. The estimate, £10.5031, is 0.7 standard errors from £10.4506.

screens.title: A suspiciously exact price
screens.prose: A colleague's pricer reports an error of zero. Here is his loop.

lines: double st = s * std::exp(drift + vol * z(gen));
params.title: mc.cpp

screens.question: Why is the standard error zero?

options.text: Every path reseeds the generator, so every path draws the same $Z$

options.why: The error falls like $1/\sqrt n$, never to zero: 20,000 paths give about £0.10.

options.text: A seeded generator is deterministic, so a seeded run has no error
options.why: A seed fixes the whole stream, not each draw. Seeded once, the draws still differ from path to path.

options.text: The distribution must be built outside the loop; the generator is fine
options.why: Moving `z` out helps, but `gen` would still restart from the same state on every path.

hints.text: Which line runs again on every pass of the loop?
Line 3 builds a fresh generator from the same seed each time.
Every path draws the first number of seed 42's stream: $Z = 0.5154$, $S_T = 114.23$, payoff £14.23, discounted £13.54.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow `gen` through two passes of the loop.

byKey.many: The error falls like $1/\sqrt n$, never to zero: 20,000 paths give about £0.10.
byKey.seeded: A seed fixes the whole stream, not each draw. Seeded once, the draws still differ from path to path.

explain.text:
Line 3 restarts the stream on every path, so all 20,000 paths are the first path: £14.23 discounted to £13.54, with no spread at all. Build the generator once, before the loop, as `terminal_prices` does.

```cpp
std::mt19937 gen(seed);                        // once
std::normal_distribution<double> z(0.0, 1.0);  // once
for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) { /* draw z(gen) */ }
```

screens.title: A payoff on the whole path
screens.prose: An **Asian** call pays the average of m monthly prices minus the strike. Our `Payoff` takes one spot, so it cannot express this: a path pricer simulates every month. With m = 12, seed 42 and 20,000 paths, a C++ program printed:
screens.question: Why is the Asian call so much cheaper?

options.text: An average of twelve monthly prices moves less than the final price does
It pays out earlier, so it is discounted less
options.why: Both pay at year end. The difference is in what they pay, not when.

options.text: Monte Carlo noise: run it again and they will agree
options.why: The gap of £4.30 is about 35 combined standard errors. It is real.
Both used 20,000 paths; the Asian one drew twelve normals per path.

hints.text: What is the volatility of an average compared with one price?
Early months of the average are close to today's £100.
Averaging smooths the path, so the payoff's spread is smaller and the option is cheaper.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare how far the average can move with how far $S_T$ can.

explain.text: The average of the monthly prices is less volatile than $S_T$, and a call's value rises with volatility. There is no simple closed form for this average, which is where Monte Carlo earns its keep.

screens.title: The estimator and its error
screens.prose: You computed $$\hat c = e^{-rT}\,\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f\big(S_T^{(i)}\big),\qquad \text{SE} = \frac{s}{\sqrt n},$$ with $s$ the sample standard deviation of the discounted payoffs. The chart shows your C++ estimate for 1,000 to 20,000 paths, seed 42, with a band of two standard errors.
screens.question: Is 10.4735 ± 0.1042 consistent with Black-Scholes, 10.4506?

options.text: Yes: it is 0.22 standard errors away

options.why: A simulated price always differs a little. The question is by how many standard errors.
It already is: the gap of £0.023 is well inside one standard error.
Simulation has error; that is what SE measures. Here the error happens to cover the gap.

hints.text: Divide the gap by the standard error.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Measure the gap in standard errors.

explain.text: The gap is £0.023, or 0.22 standard errors. At every n on the chart the band holds £10.4506, as it should about 95% of the time. A test that the price lies within 3 standard errors of a known value fails by chance only about 0.3% of the time.

screens.title: A price on a trade ticket
screens.prose: For an exotic with no closed form, the trade ticket carries the Monte Carlo price and its error. This one priced a payoff with 20,000 paths. Risk wants the error down to ± £0.02 before the trade is booked.
screens.question: How many paths does the same pricer need?

widget.label: Paths
widget.accept: 500,000: the error must fall 5 times, so the paths rise $5^2 = 25$ times

hints.text: By what factor must the error fall?
From £0.10 to £0.02 is a factor of 5.
The error goes like $1/\sqrt n$, so the paths rise $5^2 = 25$ times: $25 \times 20{,}000$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The error falls with the square root of the paths.

byKey.linear: Five times the paths cuts the error only by $\sqrt 5$, to about £0.045. It needs 25 times.
byKey.sqrt: You took $\sqrt 5$ times the paths. The paths must rise by $5^2$.

explain.text: From £0.10 to £0.02 is 5 times smaller, so $5^2 = 25$ times the paths: 500,000. Antithetic pairs would roughly halve that. Desks also swap pseudo-random draws for quasi-random sequences such as Sobol, whose error falls closer to $1/n$.

ideas: Simulate $S_T = S\exp((r - \sigma^2/2)T + \sigma\sqrt T Z)$ with one `std::mt19937` seeded once, average the payoffs and discount. Seed 42 and 20,000 paths give £10.4735 for our call.
Report the standard error $s/\sqrt n$ beside the price: £0.1042 here. Halving it costs four times the paths. Test a simulated price against a known one within 3 standard errors.
Antithetic pairs, $Z$ and $-Z$, halve the variance of our call for the same work. Path payoffs such as an Asian average need every step simulated.

formula.name: Monte Carlo price and error
formula.note: $s$ divides by $n - 1$; with $n = 1$ there is no error estimate.

summary.trap: Seeding the generator inside the loop gives every path the same draw: a price from one path and a standard error of zero.

quiz.prose: A Monte Carlo pricer prints 11.0105 for our call (seed 42, 20,000 paths). Black-Scholes says £10.4506; the correct pricer gives 10.4735 ± 0.1042.
quiz.question: What did it most likely forget?

options.why: The gap is £0.56, over five standard errors. More paths would not close it.
That would raise every path by $e^{0.02}$. Check $10.4735 \times e^{0.05}$ instead.
An unseeded `std::mt19937` uses a default seed and still gives a sound estimate.

explain.text: $11.0105 / 10.4735 = 1.0513 = e^{0.05}$: the average payoff was reported in year-end pounds. Multiply by $e^{-rT}$.

quiz.prose: With 20,000 paths, a colleague divides by $n$ instead of $n - 1$ in the sample variance.
quiz.question: How much does his standard error of £0.1042 change?

options.why: Only the divisor of the variance changes, from 19,999 to 20,000.
The relative change is about $1/(2n) = 0.0025\%$ here. It matters only for tiny samples.
The deviations are unchanged. Only the divisor moves, by one in 20,000.

explain.text: The standard error scales by $\sqrt{(n-1)/n}$, here 0.999975. With two paths the same slip cuts it by 29%, from 6.77 to 4.79.

quiz.prose: `mc_price` takes the number of paths as an `int`.
quiz.question: Up to how many paths is that safe?

options.why: That is a 16-bit limit. An `int` here is 32 bits.
That is an unsigned 64-bit limit. An `int` is signed and 32 bits here.
There is no such limit. Two billion paths would be far beyond the time budget long before overflow.

feedback.correct: Over two billion: far more paths than any run here would use.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A 32-bit signed `int` holds up to $2^{31} - 1$.

explain.text: $2^{31} - 1 = 2{,}147{,}483{,}647$. A million paths is far inside it. The sum is a `double`, so it never overflows either.

quiz.prose: Edge case: `mc_price` with `n = 1` and seed 42 returns £13.54.
quiz.question: What standard error goes with it?

options.text: None: one path gives no estimate of the spread

options.why: One value has no spread to measure, which is not the same as a spread of zero. The $n - 1$ divisor is 0.
The error measures spread between paths. One path has none to compare.
The gap to a known price is not the standard error. It needs the sample spread.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Try dividing by $n - 1$ with one path.

explain.text: With $n = 1$ the sample variance is $0/0$. Our function throws rather than report a fake zero.
